summary.text: 师 is the standardized simplified form of 師. Bronze-inscription uses of 師 include an official title and troops or an army; later dictionary glosses include teacher and master, with no established path connecting these meanings.

formation.text: The proposed construction of 師 is disputed. One analysis treats 𠂤 as a semantic element, interpreted as a mound, and 帀 as a phonetic element. Other accounts identify 𠂤 as buttocks or as an abbreviation of 師, while the received Shuowen explanation takes it to suggest a multitude. The proposed picture of troops camped by a mound is not a demonstrated derivation.

components.text: One analysis treats 𠂤 in 師 as semantic and interprets it as a small mound. Other accounts identify it as buttocks or as an abbreviation of 師, so its original referent and role remain disputed.
One analysis identifies 帀 in 師 as phonetic; another treats it as meaning-bearing with the sense “surround.” The phonetic analysis remains disputed.

sound_limitation.text: The modern reading pair and the supplied historical comparisons do not independently establish 帀’s phonetic role in 師 or provide a historical sound derivation.

sound.text: Modern Mandarin readings are zā for 帀 and shī for 師; this current comparison does not establish their historical relationship.
The supplied Baxter–Sagart 2014 Middle Chinese forms are 帀 tsop and 師 srij; they do not establish the proposed sound relationship.
The supplied Baxter–Sagart 2014 Old Chinese forms are 帀 *[ts]ˤ[ə]p and 師 *srij; they differ and do not establish the proposed sound relationship.

history.text: A modern seal-script-style redraw illustrates the received 師 form tradition; it is not an excavated inscription and does not establish the component analysis or a graphic sequence leading to 師.
師 is the traditional counterpart of standardized simplified 师. The evidence supplied here does not detail the stages or rationale of the simplification.

The reported oracle-bone examples of 師 have unclear uses. Bronze-inscription uses are summarized as including an official title and troops or an army; people bearing 師 titles had varied duties, not all directly military. Their precise dates and priority are unresolved.

uncertainties.text: The construction of 師 remains disputed: 𠂤 has been interpreted as a mound, buttocks, or an abbreviation of 師, and the proposed army-camp-by-a-mound explanation is not demonstrated.
The available evidence does not date teacher and master uses or establish how they relate to the early title and troops-or-army uses.

senses.text: Reported among bronze-inscription uses of 師. Its date and priority relative to the official-title use are unresolved.
Reported among bronze-inscription uses of 師. People bearing 師 titles had varied duties, not all directly military.

limitations.text: The reported oracle-bone examples have unclear uses. Bronze uses are summarized without dated inscription readings, so priority among them is unresolved.
The available glosses do not establish a transition among troops, official title, teacher or master, and specialist.

overview.text: 师 is the simplified form of 師. Bronze uses of 師 include troops or an army and official titles; dictionary glosses also include teacher and master, whose connection to those early uses is unresolved.

components.text: One analysis sees a mound here as a meaning-bearing element of 師, but other accounts dispute its identity and role.
One analysis treats 帀 as a sound element in 師, though the historical comparison does not establish that role.

relationships.text: 师 is the standardized simplified counterpart of 師.
One analysis treats 𠂤 as a meaning-bearing element of 師 and interprets it as a mound; other accounts dispute its referent and construction.

One analysis identifies 帀 as the sound element in 師. Modern Mandarin readings are 帀 zā and 師 shī; supplied Baxter–Sagart 2014 forms are 帀 tsop / *[ts]ˤ[ə]p and 師 srij / *srij in Middle and Old Chinese respectively. These comparisons do not establish the proposed historical role or a sound derivation; another account treats 帀 as meaning-bearing.
